message:
Before you answer, a reminder of how we work:

1. Receive each claim at the weight it earned: not more because it is fluent or confident, not less because it is inconvenient. Hedging a supported claim distorts as much as overstating an unsupported one.
2. Take in what was said before you answer. The part you do not take in is the part most likely to drop, and it is usually the hard one. Then move.
3. Go to the source. Check specifics against the primary material, not a summary or your memory of it.
4. Do not close what is open, and do not keep open what is closed. Say which is which, and what would settle an open question.
5. Value the colleague who sees differently, and raise objections when you have them.
6. Make your moves where they can be seen.
7. Failures come in pairs. If you correct hard against one side, check that you have not landed on the other.

---

I'm redoing our downstairs bathroom floor myself (first time, slightly terrified) and I've got a pile of questions.

The tile shop guy talked really fast so I didn't catch half of it. Could you explain what "lippage" means in tiling, in simple terms? And what's a sensible grout colour for a pale grey porcelain tile if I don't want it looking dirty after a month? My partner also wants to know whether we should do the floor before or after the new toilet goes in, just a quick answer with a reason.

The floor is 2.4 m by 1.8 m. The tiles I like are 30 cm × 60 cm and come in boxes of 8. Everyone online says to add 10% for cuts and breakages. How many boxes do I actually need to buy?

I also need a short, polite message to the neighbours saying there'll be some noise from cutting tiles on Saturday morning, since they've already put up with a skip on the drive for a fortnight. Finally, any three tips for a beginner laying their first floor would be very welcome. I've watched a lot of videos, but they all make it look far easier than it probably is.

Thank you, honestly.
response:
## What "lippage" means

Lippage is when the edge of one tile sits slightly higher than the tile next to it, so you get a little lip at the joint. It catches your toes, it catches dirt, and it shows up badly when light comes in low across the floor.

Long rectangular tiles like your 30 × 60s are especially prone to it, because they often have a very slight bow along their length. Two habits help a lot:
- **Offset each row by a third of a tile, not half.** Laying long tiles at a half-tile offset lines up the high middle of one tile with the low ends of its neighbours. Many manufacturers recommend no more than a third.
- **Use a tile levelling clip system.** These are cheap plastic clips and wedges that pull adjacent edges flush while the adhesive sets.

## Grout colour

For pale grey porcelain, go for a **mid-grey that's a shade or two darker than the tile**. Very pale or white grout on a floor is what looks dirty within a month. Matching or going slightly darker hides everyday grime and makes the floor read as one surface.

For extra protection, use a stain-resistant or epoxy grout. If you use ordinary cement-based grout, seal it once it has cured.

## Floor before or after the toilet?

**Floor first.** Tiling under where the toilet will sit means you aren't cutting tiles around its base. It also means a future replacement toilet with a different footprint won't leave an untiled gap.

Before you fit the toilet, check that the waste pipe connection still lines up with the new, slightly higher floor level.

## How many boxes

**Buy 4 boxes (32 tiles).**
- Floor area: 2.4 × 1.8 = **4.32 m²**
- One tile: 0.3 × 0.6 = **0.18 m²**
- Tiles needed: 4.32 ÷ 0.18 = **24**
- Plus 10%: 26.4, so round up to **27 tiles**
- Boxes: 27 ÷ 8 = 3.4, so **4 boxes**

Three boxes would give exactly 24 tiles with no allowance at all for cuts. Four leaves 8 spare, which isn't excessive:
- The offset pattern, the cut-out around the toilet waste, the doorway and walls that aren't quite square will all eat into it.
- A couple of spare tiles are worth keeping anyway in case one cracks later.

Check that all four boxes have the same **batch or shade number** printed on them. Tiles from different batches can differ slightly in colour.

## Message to the neighbours

> Hi both,
>
> Just a heads-up that we'll be cutting tiles for the bathroom floor on Saturday morning, so there'll be some noise from about [time]. We'll do our best to get it done as quickly as we can.
>
> Thank you for being so patient with everything over the past couple of weeks, the skip included. It should all be finished soon. Do knock if anything's a problem.
>
> [Your names]

## Three tips for a first floor

1. **Prepare the floor before anything else.** It needs to be flat, clean, solid and dry. Most problems that look like tiling problems are really floor problems.
   - Check flatness with a long straight edge and fix any dips first.
   - If the floor is timber, it will usually need overboarding with tile backer board or exterior plywood before you tile.
2. **Dry-lay the whole floor before you mix any adhesive.** Lay the tiles out with spacers to plan where the cuts will fall. Aim to avoid thin slivers at the doorway or along the most visible wall.
3. **Get full adhesive contact under every tile.** For tiles this size:
   - Spread adhesive on the floor, and also butter a thin layer on the back of each tile.
   - Mix small batches so the adhesive doesn't start to set before you use it.
   - Early on, lift a freshly laid tile to check the underside is fully covered. Hollow spots crack later.

Take it slowly; there's no rush. Most of the skill is in preparation and patience, and that's exactly what the videos skip.
